Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) Bill 2019, Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2019 - in Committee - Oversight

The majority voted against an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2019-07-25.242.1) introduced by by Tasmanian Senator [Nick McKim](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/tasmania/nick_mckim) (Greens), which means it failed. Senator McKim [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2019-07-25.242.1): > *These amendments, importantly, would provide for crossbench membership on the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security and help that committee to do its job, to scrutinise the ongoing march of this country down the road to a police state.*

The speaker moved the second reading of the Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) Bill 2019, arguing it would allow authorities to delay the return of Australians of counterterrorism concern for up to two years and impose conditions on return, citing that around 230 Australians had travelled to Syria or Iraq since 2012 with about 80 still active. The bill includes independent review of ministerial decisions and a return permit process.

The Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2019 was introduced to add accountability and transparency measures to the temporary exclusion order scheme, implementing recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security. It amends the Intelligence Services Act 2001 to give the committee monitoring and review powers, requires a review of the scheme within three years, and allows the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor to review the scheme on their own initiative.

The government has rejected at least 10 bipartisan recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security on the Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) Bill 2019 without explanation, breaching a long-standing compact on national security legislation. The bill should be amended to conform to the committee's recommendations and referred back for further scrutiny.

The speaker argued in favour of the Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) Bill 2019 and against the Isaacs amendment, citing 16 disrupted terrorist attacks since 2014, nearly 230 Australian citizens who travelled to Syria and Iraq, and approximately 80 still active in conflict zones, while detailing the bill's provisions for ministerial discretion, judicial review, and child-specific safeguards.

The speaker argued that the government's temporary exclusion orders bill ignores recommendations from its own parliamentary committee and lacks long-term deradicalisation and international coordination strategies, despite $13 million promised for deradicalisation programs and $60 million for counter-terrorism.

The speaker argued for the Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) Bill 2019, which would allow the minister to control the return of Australian citizens of counterterrorism interest from overseas conflict zones, citing around 230 Australians who have travelled to Syria or Iraq since 2012.

The speaker argued that the Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) Bill 2019 is essential to delay, control and risk-manage the return of foreign fighters, and expressed support for the bill in its present form while opposing Labor's amendments. The speaker noted that the parliamentary committee made 18 recommendations, including judicial review (recommendation 7), which the government accepted in principle, and cited an operational imperative to pass the bill.

The speaker argued that the Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) Bill 2019 gives the minister unchecked power to bar Australian citizens from returning to the country without any crime or judicial review, undermining the rule of law and democracy. They supported opposition amendments to improve the bill and criticised the government for using it to wedge Labor, warning that it could apply to children as young as 14.

The speaker argued that the Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2019 must be passed to introduce accountability and transparency measures for the temporary exclusion order scheme, including monitoring by a committee and the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor within three years.

Migration Amendment (Strengthening the Character Test) Bill 2019 - Second Reading - Agree with bill's main idea

The same number of senators voted for and against a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2021-10-20.18.6) to agree with main idea of [the bill](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr6349%22), which means the motion failed. In parliamentary jargon, they declined to read the bill for a [second time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/). This means that the bill will no longer be considered and will not become law. ### What is the bill's main idea? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1920a/20bd012): > *The purpose of the Migration Amendment (Strengthening the Character Test) Bill 2019 (the Bill) is to amend the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) (the Act) to specify that a person does not pass the character test—and may have their visa cancelled or visa application refused—if they have been convicted of a ‘designated offence’.* A 'designated offence' is [defined in proposed subsection 501(7AA)](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1920a/20bd012#_Toc14860870) as "*an offence against a law in force in Australia or a foreign country, which:* * *involves one or more of a list of specified ‘physical elements’ and* * *is punishable by a maximum or fixed term of imprisonment of not less than two years.*" ### *** Caution *** The voting data for this division is currently incorrect. It appears to have been flipped. The Coalition should be marked as voting "Yes" (it's their bill) with the Opposition etc. voting "No". See the [Hansard](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Hansard/Hansard_Display?bid=chamber/hansards/25180/&sid=0000) for the correct voting data.

The Migration Amendment (Strengthening the Character Test) Bill 2019 was moved to amend section 501 of the Migration Act, creating an objective ground for visa refusal or cancellation for non-citizens convicted of designated offences carrying a maximum sentence of at least two years, including violence, sexual offences, weapon offences, and protection order breaches.

Labor argued it will oppose the Migration Amendment (Strengthening the Character Test) Bill 2019, calling it unnecessary and ill-considered, and noted the bill is opposed by the New Zealand government, the Law Council of Australia, the Australian Human Rights Commission, and numerous other organisations, with no supporters outside the government.

The Migration Amendment (Strengthening the Character Test) Bill 2019 is necessary to keep Australia safe by identifying and removing non-citizens who do not respect the country, and it will help mitigate terrorism risks.

The speaker argued the Migration Amendment (Strengthening the Character Test) Bill 2019 is unnecessary because existing law already gives the minister broad powers to cancel visas, and the bill would harm Australia–New Zealand relations. Labor will oppose the bill unless the government adopts three amendments to avoid retrospective liability, exclude trivial offences from the character test, and review ministerial decisions on New Zealanders' visas; 16 of 17 submissions opposed the bill, with only one in support.

The speaker supported the Migration Amendment (Strengthening the Character Test) Bill 2019, which adds a list of designated offences so that anyone convicted of these crimes in Australia or overseas automatically fails the character test, and criticised Labor for siding with the New Zealand government instead of prioritising Australian safety.

The speaker argued the Migration Amendment (Strengthening the Character Test) Bill 2019 is unnecessary because the minister already has broad discretion to cancel visas for serious criminals—4,700 visas have been cancelled since 2014—and criticised the bill as a political wedge that risks retroactive punishment, captures low-level offending, and damages Australia’s relationship with New Zealand.

The speech argued that the Migration Amendment (Strengthening the Character Test) Bill 2019 should be passed to allow visa cancellation or refusal for non‑citizens convicted of specific serious offences (including violence, sexual offences, and weapon offences), regardless of sentence length. The speaker also criticised the Labor Party for opposing the bill, alleging that Labor would allow such offenders to remain in Australia.

Labor will oppose the Migration Amendment (Strengthening the Character Test) Bill 2019 unless the government removes its unintended consequences, arguing existing Migration Act powers are sufficient and the new "designated offences" definition ignores actual court sentences, risking deportation of low-level offenders. The bill could further strain relations with New Zealand and the Pacific, citing 1,600 New Zealand visa cancellations in four years, Jacinda Ardern's "corrosive" criticism, and only 203 Pacific Labour Scheme visas granted against 185,000 backpacker visas.

The Labor member argued the Migration Amendment (Strengthening the Character Test) Bill is redundant because the minister already has broad powers under sections 501 and 116 of the Migration Act to cancel or refuse visas on character grounds, and the bill is a political tactic to demonise migrants. Labor will not support the bill in its current form, citing issues such as retrospective double jeopardy, and has proposed conditions the government must meet for its support.

The speaker argued the Migration Amendment (Strengthening the Character Test) Bill 2019 would dangerously expand ministerial power by lowering the threshold for visa cancellations, removing accountability and appeal rights. They also claimed the government is using the bill to politically wedge Labor, while noting citizenship applications backlogged from 27,000 in 2013 to 221,000 by June 2019.

The Migration Amendment (Strengthening the Character Test) Bill 2019 would allow the government to cancel visas of non-citizens convicted of serious crimes—including violence, sexual offences, breaching protection orders, or unlawful weapon use—where the maximum sentence is two years or more, even if the actual sentence is under 12 months. The speaker argued the opposition's refusal to support the bill is extraordinary.

The speaker supported the Defence Amendment (Call Out of the Australian Defence Force) Bill 2018, arguing it updates the legal framework for deploying the ADF domestically against terrorism, citing the 1978 Hilton bombing, the 1995 Aum Shinrikyo attack, and the 2014 Lindt Cafe siege as examples of evolving threats. He noted the bill expands ADF powers to search, detain persons, and operate across multiple jurisdictions, while maintaining civilian primacy and democratic oversight.

The speaker argued that the Nationals have failed to plan for worsening drought conditions driven by climate change, citing damage to the APVMA, removal of the inspector-general for live exports, and inadequate water management. He advocated for long-term support measures such as the Carbon Farming Initiative and aggregated farming systems, noting that 88% of surveyed farmers want politicians to do more on climate change.
Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Competition and Consumer) Bill 2018

The speech supported the amendment to the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Competition and Consumer) Bill 2017, arguing the Coalition's multi-technology NBN approach has caused service failures, digital divides (e.g., Queanbeyan/Jerrabomberra and the Barton Highway), satellite congestion, and cost overruns. It called for an independent expert review of the NBN satellite service, more fixed wireless towers, and cited examples such as birdsnest in Cooma and the original plan's estimated $60 billion economic benefit.

The speaker argued for the Security of Critical Infrastructure Bill 2018, citing threats from state-sponsored cyberattacks (including Vladimir Putin’s Russia) and deficiencies in the Foreign Investment Review Board process (Port of Darwin, Ausgrid, Global Switch). He urged improving energy security by setting a target to end oil dependence, pointing to health costs (3,000 Australian deaths per year from vehicle emissions) and parallel international bans on petrol and diesel.
Intelligence Services Amendment (Establishment of the Australian Signals Directorate) Bill 2018

The speaker supported the Intelligence Services Amendment (Establishment of the Australian Signals Directorate) Bill 2018, noting it resolved internal ASD issues and was bipartisan; they also highlighted the need to share cybersecurity skills with private industry, citing a Data61 PhD student assisting the AFP, and praised the Information Warfare Division under Major General Thompson.

The speaker argued that the Intelligence Services Amendment Bill received full Labor cooperation, noted no change to ASD's role supporting Defence, and highlighted workforce challenges for security agencies. Concrete points include: ASD reports directly to the defence minister; an Information Warfare Division led by Major General Thompson (PhD in cybersecurity, special forces) will grow from 100 to about 900 personnel by the end of the decade, requiring a supply pool of around 3,000; and comparisons were drawn to Singapore's national service and Israel's Talpiot program.
